text.p: A Ukrainian cabinet reshuffle on Wednesday did little to dispel economic uncertainty in this former Soviet republic even though President Leonid Kuchma said the shakeup was aimed at speeding up the reform process.
A presidential aide said the clear-out was not over after Kuchma moved one minister to a new post and sacked three more, accusing his finance minister of "serious inadequacies".

"The economic block has stopped developing, so new forces are essential," Kuchma told a news conference in the western Ukrainian city of Lviv where he was on holiday and meeting Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi.
He singled out the ministry of machine-building, the military complex and conversion whose new leader is Vasyl Hureyev sacked on Tuesday from the economy ministry.

But Kuchma did not comment on the ministries of finance, economy and statistics whose chiefs were also swept out by decree on Tuesday, saying simply: "We must move from administrative forms of management to economic ones".
Political analysts said the reshuffle reflected political rivalries and was unlikely to help the economy.
Some said the action might unsettle the atmosphere at a time when Kiev is seeking a new multi-billion-dollar loan from the International Monetary Fund.

But the secretary of the policy-making security and defence council said more dismissals could follow. "These are essential changes and these changes will continue," Volodymyr Horbulin, Kuchma's closest aide, told a news briefing.
Horbulin made clear that Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko, whose criticism of the ministers at a cabinet session last Friday preceded the dismissals, was safe for the time being.
"Two or three days ago the Ukrainian prime minister said his own position was fairly stable. I agree with him," he said.
Analysts interpreted the sackings as a pre-emptive strike to save Lazarenko amid a raft of economic troubles which has brought miners, teachers and other workers on to the streets.

A cash crisis has left workers unpaid for months, gross domestic product was down 10.4 percent last month compared to January last year and the government has failed so far to win parliamentary approval for this year's budget and tax reforms.
But economists said the real problems lay in the economy itself and sacking ministers would not help, particularly when new policies were being put in place.
"This is unnerving and unsettling. It can't be a good thing, in that there's no stability and continuity," one analyst said.
"I can't imagine the IMF believe that their replacements will be the salvation of the Ukrainian economy," he added.
Ukraine hopes to win a $2.5 billion to $3 billion Extended Fund Facility loan from the IMF this year to take over from a $860 million stand-by loan.
Ukrainian currency dealers said the sacking of finance minister Valentyn Koronevsky would have no impact on the Treasury-bill and currency markets as he did not define policies in those areas.
Kuchma, Lazarenko and central bank chief Viktor Yushchenko are seen as controlling financial and economic policies.
Mityukov, who was also deputy head of the central bank and currently represents Ukraine's interests at the European Union, was seen as the only viable alternative to Koronevsky.
